utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Call the listed in motion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-97-24-PT, Prosecutor versus Milan Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann, I appear with my colleagues Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, Mr. Morten Bergsmo and Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You should press the button that brings the red light on.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: The red light is on. Thank you, I am sorry for that. Good morning your Honours, my name is Anthony D'Amato, lead counsel for Dr Kovacevic. My co-counsel are here this morning, Mr. Igor Pantelic, Mr. Dusan Vucicevic, and Mr. Simor Vucinic is, I presume, being robed. May I ask the court for the doctor, our client, to confirm the appearance of the co-counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Dr Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What should I say, that these are my attorneys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I understand, incidentally, that there is some question of precisely the status of your colleagues, but there is no objection, certainly, to them being seated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think in view of the fact that there was some confusion with a press announcement that was made early yesterday, followed by an amended one, that it is probably desirable just to state what the current situation is and what we are dealing with. Altogether, there are three motions that have been -- there are four, but we can deal only with three of them, that were filed by the Defence. There was the motion to clarify standards, if I can use the short title, and that has already been disposed of by an order of 1st October, although that did not appear in the initial press release. Then there is a motion to strike portions of the indictment, and that motion will not be heard by this Chamber. The indictment is, in any event, to be amended in due course, whatever that may mean, and the members of this Chamber now sitting will not form the Trial Chamber. I retire in November and my two colleagues will not be hearing this matter after November. Accordingly, it will be dealt with by whatever new Chamber, new Trial Chamber is constituted by the new President in November. I note, however, that the Prosecutor, as I understand it, has agreed to remove Simo Drljaca as co-accused; that is correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Presumably that includes paragraphs 3 to 5 of the indictment and all references to him in the remainder of the indictment, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly all references to him in the remainder of the indictment, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think 3 to 5 deal exclusively with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. That therefore leaves, as far as that motion is concerned, the background and the heading "superior authority". The typographical error in the indictment in paragraph 7 was amended, it seems, at the initial appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If I can just finish, but it is going to require, in any event, I think, substantial further amendment if paragraphs 3 to 5 are in fact to be omitted, because it will not stand on its own. Yes, Mr. D'Amato, you were going to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Yes. Was there an order of the court with respect to the change that was requested by Prosecutor at the hearing when they amended, as they say, the typographical -- was there an order of the court, because I did not receive any such order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps you can elucidate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It was by consent, as I understand it, your Honour. We raised the matter and it was consented to by the Defence. The court merely accepted that at the time and I think that can be taken as though it was accepted by the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You were not counsel at that time, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: No, your Honour, but since I did not receive an order I would like to then request the Prosecution, if you could then prepare an order, in conformity with the consent. We will have no objection, of course, so that I could have an order of the court requiring the change, as opposed to the transcript, which also I have not received. It would just be good to have this reduced to a court order, if there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think we can deal with that in the status conference that follows this application, because if there is going to be a considerable amendment to the indictment, it can be taken up at that time. Then there remains the motion as to non-disclosure and provisional release, and that is the motion that we will now hear and that appears in the scheduling order of 1st October. As to one portion of it, the non-disclosure of the indictment, as I understand it, that has already been vacated by decision of 10th July of Judge Odio Benito, and if that is so, and I would like confirmation of that from counsel on both sides, there remains really only the matter of provisional release, which we will hear this morning. Is that your understanding, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that it has been vacated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: No, it is not my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What is your understanding?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: My understanding is that there are continuing ramifications of the order. Damage being done is still being done and then the order to vacate, while perfectly proper in its own step, does not affect my motion today to have that overruled, to say that the order ordering concealment should be overturned by this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think there may be a procedural difficulty how we overturn an order that has been vacated, I am not sure, but we will hear your submissions when we come to that. Mr. Niemann, on this question then of provisional release and, to the extent to which it is relevant, the non-disclosure aspect, we will now hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does your Honour wish to hear me first or the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think we should probably -- as to the non-disclosure, have you anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Only, your Honours, that our position is that the non-disclosure order has been vacated. It is contained, your Honour, in our written motion, in paragraph 9. Your Honour, we refer to the fact that the non-disclosure order relating to the accused was vacated on 10th July, the date of the accused's arrest. It had to be vacated on that date because of the arrest and it follows that that happened then. Her Honour made an order on that day. So far as we are concerned, your Honour, that matter has now been disposed of, and I am interested to hear argument as to how it is that the Chamber can then proceed to deal with it, seeing as it has been vacated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The only other matter that perhaps I might raise while I am on my feet is that as I have understood the motion that has been filed by the Defence in this matter, the motion is preconditioned on vacating of the order for provisional release under Rule 65 and has, by their motion, been preconditioned on the vacating of the order by Judge Odio Benito. So my understanding of the situation is this, that if that matter is not disposed of, then the basis upon which their application under Rule 65 for provisional release falls too, because they say, if I might just take your Honour to it, they say in their motion, on page 2, your Honour, at about point 8 of the page: "The defendant does not ask this Tribunal to reconsider its order for detention of 30th July 1997. Rather the defendant requests that the Tribunal, if it should grant the defendant's motion to overrule Judge Odio Benito's order of 13th March 1997, issue a new order of provisional release under Rule 65." On the basis of the way that is structured, it is my understanding of the matter that it only -- consideration of provisional release, so far as this motion is concerned, only arises if your Honours are to overrule the order of Judge Odio Benito. As I say, that order has been vacated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: On a strict matter of construction, I suppose that may be so, but I take it that you are prepared today to deal with the application for provisional release regardless of the particular construction that I think you rightly place on the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, thank you. Yes, Mr. D'Amato.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: If I may address that last remark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I should say to save time that as far as I am concerned, and I would like to consult with my fellow judges, but we would not hold you to that strict construction. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Okay, I appreciate that. In any event, for the record I want the Prosecution, since the Prosecution is violently objected to the coupling of those two points, the Prosecution should not be allowed to say the opposite today. That is all I wanted to say for the record, but I would be glad to proceed with the argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Is it your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Incidentally, in argument, you might bear in mind that we have, of course, read the grounds stated in the motion and mere repetition is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Good, I appreciate that. Then let me begin by addressing the motion to overrule the concealed indictment on the basis of the Prosecution's objections, which the court has read. In the first place, the Prosecution places on this the idea that the concealed indictment is simply a matter of formality, no particular harm was done, it is just a trivial administrative convenience, and in any event it has been vacated. I beg to differ with that assertion. In the first place, considerable harm was done to the defendant by virtue of this concealed indictment. He was deprived of the chance, the opportunity, of submitting himself voluntarily to this Tribunal. Instead, and we have several witnesses for this, and if the court wishes we will obtain our affidavits when our counsel goes into the field to investigate the case, the defendant was arrested and taken to Tuzla, where he was then put down on the ground and put into a container, a 18 foot metal container that is used for storage. This was on July 10th at the heat of noon in Bosnia. It was extraordinarily hot outside. When he was put in the container, he was asked to stand facing the wall. The container has a heating element in it in order to prevent stored materials from freezing in the winter. The radiator was turned on. The defendant was then facing a wall, standing up, for two hours in this intense heat while the indictment was read to him. At the end of which time, he was put in a helicopter and taken to Amsterdam -- put on a plane and taken to Amsterdam. In coming off the plane, he suffered a stroke; that is, a deprivation of blood to the brain, paralysis in the limbs. Under the Convention on Torture, this might be construed as the deliberate infliction of bodily harm on a person presumed to be innocent by government officials with consequent severe physical damage, but I am not here to argue the construction of Article 1 of the Convention on Torture. I am just pointing out that harm was done. More importantly, what about harm today? What is the continuing harm of this concealed indictment and the fact that the defendant was deprived of the opportunity to submit voluntarily? Excuse me, please. (Pause). Just last week, the newspapers reported the war crimes suspects taken to this Tribunal, and an Associated Press despatch quoted the United States State Department's spokesman James Foley saying that the United States: "... pledges to make every effort to strengthen the Tribunal's resources ..." In parentheses, which I completely applaud, I am totally in favour to that: "... to facilitate speedy trials for all indictees, particularly those who surrender voluntarily." In other words, by being deprived of the opportunity to surrender voluntarily, Dr Kovacevic is not one of those people to whom a speedy trial is being promised under this new statement of last week, and indeed his trial might even be held up in order to accommodate the speedy trial of the people who were voluntarily arrested. This is a tremendous prejudicial harm to my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is a statement by the US government, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: That is right, it is not binding on the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It has no relevance as far as the Tribunal is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Excellent. Then I do not have to worry about it. Thank you, that certainly clears that up. The decision to conceal the indictment in the first place I argue was arbitrary, because there is no evidence that has been provided to me of any evidence whatsoever of the doctor's danger to any other persons, danger to any potential witnesses, any potential of fleeing. Your Honours have read my motion, and without repeating it, just to summarise very briefly, every day the doctor went on his job at the hospital in Prijedor; he was an open public figure, there was no need to arrest him surreptitiously and cause this damage that I have already recounted to you. On many occasions he said if he were indicted he would come voluntarily and we can provide evidence of that if you need, because he said it in many public places. In addition, we have to take as part of our understanding of this entire case -- we can not understand this case without looking at what the indictment is. The indictment says nothing about Dr Kovacevic's presence at any crimes of genocide, it says nothing about his participation in any crimes of genocide, there is no factual allegation that connects him to any acts of genocide whatsoever. The entire case, at least as far as I have heard it, and there may be more evidence forthcoming, but the entire case as far as I have seen it in all the records and all the presentation to Judge Odio Benito in her consideration of the concealed indictment, simply says that as a matter of de jure construction that the doctor was in a chain of command relating to the genocide, but that is not a fact, that is a presumption. That has to be shown at trial. I am not going to argue the trial here, but I simply want to tell you that this is not a person who has been connected with genocide, and therefore should have been given every reasonable right and dignity as a human being, all of that which was stripped away from him by an order of concealed service of the indictment that had all these consequences and was not based on any fact. I asked the very first day I came here, September 4th, I asked the Registrar, please give me a transcript of that portion of the hearing on March 13th that has to do with the concealed indictment. Here we are, a month and a week later, I have received nothing. The Prosecution have been ordered to turn this over to me, they have not given me a thing. I think this court can now take it as a matter of law, as a presumption, that there is nothing for them to give me. In other words, the record, since it has not been turned over to me, and I asked for it a month and a week ago, that there is nothing there to support Judge Odio Benito's decision to conceal the indictment. If there were, I should have received it by now. They are estopped at this point to come in with anything. On that basis, too, I argue that the decision to order a concealed indictment was arbitrary and should be overturned by this court, because of the lingering effects, because -- to keep the record straight et cetera, all the reasons that I have presented. Your Honour, let me ask you, would you like me to continue with the second part of my argument or would you like to break it up and have him respond to this and then me continue the second half?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think the latter course would probably be preferable. I suspect that the Prosecution would wish here and now to deal with what you described as the "concealed indictment".

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: I thought so, too, your Honour, and therefore I wanted to give them the opportunity to break up, with the reservation that I might come in then afterwards and deal with the second half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps before we do that, you might explain why you describe it as a "concealed indictment". Are you suggesting that there is some entitlement of an accused person to have an indictment made public in advance?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: No, what I am suggesting is that there is -- that the way this operated is that concealed indictment led to his what I call torture at Tuzla, it led to his deprivation of being allowed to come forward voluntarily, which he would have done if there had been a public indictment. In other words, the consequences attendant upon the concealed indictment caused harm and are causing continuing harm and therefore the decision to conceal, while it may have seemed like an administrative step at the time, had enormously prejudicial and adverse consequences to my client. Therefore, since the decision was not supported by any reason, it should not have been given in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I should just ask Mr. Niemann if he would like to deal with this aspect first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour. Your Honours, just to deal with the last question about the transcript, the transcript is attached to our motion, as an attachment to our motion, which was filed on 23rd September 1997 and presumably has been available to the Defence at least from that time, if not earlier. The facts that were outlined by Mr. D'Amato in relation to the arrest are not admitted as such by the Prosecution, because we, of course, did not attend that particular part of the process, the initial part of the process. That was carried out by SFOR pursuant to the provisions of the Dayton Agreement, your Honours, so I am unable to deal with them at the moment. I would presume to proceed to have those matters investigated in any event. Your Honours, the assertion by the Defence that this was an unwarranted approach to be taken by the Prosecution could not be further from the truth. Unfortunately we have had a very unfortunate history in the Republika Srpska, within that area classified as the Republika Srpska, in terms of effecting arrests and the government of that territory have indicated on numerous occasions that they will not participate or facilitate in the arrests or in the transfer of indicted war criminals to -- persons accused of being war criminals to the Tribunal. It is on the basis of that and on the fact that notwithstanding numerous public indictments having been issued by the Prosecutor in relation to people who are living in that area, and because of the totally unsuccessful attempt to have persons brought from that area to the Tribunal which gave rise to the approach taken in this case. It has almost been posited by the Defence, your Honours, that there is some right to a public indictment. I do acknowledge, your Honours, that the rules envisage that the indictment will be public, but it also envisages circumstances where that would not be so, and in my submission a history of unsuccessful attempts for people to be brought to the Tribunal who have been indicted would well and truly justify the course, in my submission, which was taken. Your Honours, in most jurisdictions the procedure is quite different to what occurs in the Tribunal in terms of arresting accused persons. In most instances, in most jurisdictions, people are arrested and they do not know about the fact that they are going to be arrested first and it is after that that they are informed of what they have been arrested for, and it is for that reason, your Honours, that there is numerous pieces of legislation throughout the world, and included in the Articles of this Tribunal, which provide expressly that upon arrest a person is to be fully informed of the basis of the arrest and informed of their rights. In my submission, it is because of that, because of the fact that arrests may take place without them knowing, the basis or the reason for it, they are taken by surprise, that these provisions are provided for. So quite contrary to what is being asserted here, your Honours, there is nothing unusual about it. In fact, it is standard procedure for it to happen this way. It is only in minor offences that we have situations where people receive summonses where it is anticipated that they might come to the court and have the matter dealt with, but in most serious cases, in the vast majority of them, people receive no notice before. Just dealing perhaps, your Honours, with a couple of the matters that were raised in the motion itself, and I rely on the submissions set out in our written motion, but perhaps if I can just touch upon a couple of them? In the written motion, reference is made in paragraph A2 to the fact that the defendant has indicated that he would be prepared to surrender to the Tribunal voluntarily. All I can say to that, your Honour, is that this is not something that has ever been conveyed to the Office of the Prosecutor and indeed if it had been conveyed to the Office of the Prosecutor, I can see that there would be a great deal of merit in the application that is presently being made by the accused in this case, in this motion. So therefore, in relation to paragraph 3, where it is asserted that it is foreseeable, in light of the facts in paragraph 2, the defendant would offer no resistance to being arrested, that he would have submitted himself. It cannot be foreseeable if that has not been conveyed. Indeed, I think, your Honours, it has occurred on occasions when people have voluntarily submitted themselves who have not been indicted and sought information about themselves, and those cases have been dealt with,. I will not go into any detail in relation to them, but it is not totally beyond the realms of reasonableness that a person could actually do that, if they wanted to forego the possibility of arrest in circumstances where they are not aware of it beforehand. In my submission, the accused did not do that in this case. If he had done so, things may well have been different. There is a reference then in paragraph 5, your Honours, to the fact that he was arrested at his place of work. I might just say to that, your Honours, that it is not unusual for people to be arrested at their place of work. Likewise, it is not unusual for a person to be arrested at their home. It is not unusual for a person to be arrested while they are travelling from work to home, but in those places, there is nothing in particular that I would submit that needs to be said about that. Finally, your Honours, in paragraph 6, reference is made to the fact that the concealed indictment has somehow damaged his character. I find that hard to understand, how that could be so. In my submission, your Honour, perhaps it may be argued that the indictment somehow damaged his character. That is perhaps the unfortunate consequences of legal proceedings being commenced against a person, but I can hardly see how concealing the indictment would achieve that end, and so in my submission, your Honours, I submit that paragraph 6 is ill-founded. Finally, your Honour, on the question of exceptional circumstances --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That is perhaps getting into the second aspect, is it not, of provisional release?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it has been raised in paragraph 5, I think, of A, A5. It is raised in paragraph 4, where he says: "The decision ordering a concealed indictment was not based on any exceptional circumstance." Just dealing quickly with that matter, your Honours, if I can take your Honours to Rule 53 of the Rules, it is our submission that the exceptional circumstances requirement relate only to paragraph A, and in our submission, paragraph A concerns itself with general non-disclosure of documents or information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. B, which deals with non-disclosure of an indictment, does not refer to any special circumstances. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what I wish to say on those matters at this stage, if your Honours please. Unless there are any other matters I can help on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato, you might like to reply very briefly to those aspects before we get on to the application for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will confine myself only to two very new points which were raised and I will not attempt to rebut the arguments, which -- I take it the court is sufficiently aware of the arguments on both sides. The first new point was the generous concession by the Prosecution that indeed everything we say might have been true and might have been avoided had the defendant only given notice to this Tribunal and to the Prosecution that he would be willing, if arrested, to come voluntarily. Unfortunately -- and I appreciate that -- but unfortunately it flies totally in the face of common sense. Dr Kovacevic heard that his name had been mentioned in the Tadic trial by various witnesses and so he was under some notice that possibly the Tribunal might try to arrest him, but since he felt that he was totally innocent there was absolutely nothing of any evidentiary value against him, he would like to have his name cleared, so if he had been arrested by a public indictment, that would have been fine, he would have come here and defended himself. But for him to give notice to the Tribunal, "guess what, I heard that my name was brought up and frankly if you arrest me I will come voluntarily", would be concession, a concession that there is something that he has to hide. If he feels he is totally innocent, he would never make such a statement, so the Prosecution's counter-factual scenario is, I think, ill-conceived, even though I appreciate the generosity of the spirit in which it was given, namely that our arguments are indeed valid and should be thought of in that respect. Secondly, the Prosecution said no harm was done by the doctor having been arrested at his place of work. He could have been arrested at home, could have been arrested on travel. No harm to the doctor; but this is a Tribunal that deals with human rights. The entire purpose of these proceedings is to protect the human rights of people. What about the human rights of patients at the hospital who were being attended to and cared for at the very time the doctor was pulled out of that hospital? How many patients at that hospital received the wrong anaesthesia because the doctor was in the middle of the process of prescribing them? He was a specialist in anaesthesia. Do we not care about their human rights too? He did not have to be arrested during the course of work when he is attending sick people. He is a man of healing. Why did we not accord him the dignity of waiting until the day was over? That was why it was very offensive to arrest him at his place of work. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. D'Amato, you might deal --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You might deal with the application for provisional release and, of course, you are aware of the terms of Rule 65 dealing with this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, your Honour. Because your Honour has introduced Rule 65, let me take a moment to open to it. As your Honour has already indicated, this Tribunal is willing to look at this question de novo, as indeed it has a right to do and a responsibility to do at any time, at any time provisional release could be granted, so it really does not have to be contingent to previous submissions, that would be a highly technical way of looking at it, so let us for the moment put aside the first half of the argument and look at this as a de novo matter. The rules of this Tribunal, which say in Rule B: "Release may be ordered by a Trial Chamber only in exceptional circumstances." I submit with all respect to the judges who formulated these rules, to all the scholars who looked at them, with the deepest respect for their learning and integrity, I submit that the ruling flies in the face of the International Covenant of Civil and Human Rights entered into force since 1976. In the International Covenant of Civil and Human Rights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think I should stop you there. As far as this Trial Chamber is concerned, for my part anyway, I would regard myself as bound by the present rules and whatever attack may be made on those rules is not really in my view for this chamber. I do not know whether my colleagues agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: That is fine, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I note your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Let me then simply reserve that point and proceed. I accept that. What are the exceptional circumstances, then, that fit this requirement? First of all is the fact -- is the doctor's medical condition, partly as a result of that stroke, which now has changed his physical condition, and I would like to introduce, on this point alone, a member of my Defence team who is also a medical doctor, is also an anaesthesiologist, and is qualified just to say a few words about the doctor's present condition which indicates that his continued detention in the detention centre may be detrimental to his health, if not his continuing existence as a defendant in this case. Is it possible that I may ask Mr. Vucicevic to say a few words on this particular score?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I see some movement on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is highly unusual. Is counsel being called as a witness, because that is the only basis on which we would agree to this sort of material being presented before the Chamber. If it is counsel is being called as a witness, then I regard it as most inappropriate, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think there are some problems in the course that you are proposing. I could understand it if you want some of the gentlemen who are with you to make submissions, but it sounds to me, and it sounded also to the Prosecution, as if you are going to call evidence. There are clear procedures of this Tribunal for joint medical inspection. Nothing whatever has been done in that respect as far as the Defence is concerned. The only medical material we have is an exhibit, I think it is annex C to the response to your motion, which includes a certificate by two medical doctors to the effect that there was no life-threatening situation and Mr. Kovacevic's appearance in court is medically not unjustified. We would not hear evidence in this way without any opportunity given to the Prosecution to have alternative medical examinations. If you have co-counsel who wishes to make some submissions on this aspect, we will certainly hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Let me say that this came up only yesterday and so what you have is not current information. I thought just for the convenience and efficiency of the proceedings that a doctor might be able to tell that to you in fewer words than I could, but if you want me to try I will try my best. I would appreciate if Mr. Vucicevic could say a few words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: If we hear him, we do not hear him as a doctor, we hear him as counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Excellent. I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, might I just raise a matter, if I may? I did not object to certain materials of fact being raised by Mr. D'Amato in the initial submissions that he made, because it was sensible that he should be able to say those things in support of the argument that he was presenting, but in relation to medical evidence about the condition of the accused, this is a very different matter, and it needs to be subjected to cross-examination and analysis and the Prosecution may wish to call its own witnesses. All of these issues arise. If counsel is now going to give facts or medical opinion about the accused, rather than just plain submissions, then I must object to those, your Honour, on that basis. I do not know what is going to happen, so perhaps I am premature, but in that event, I will foreshadow the objection I will be making, if your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think your objection would be well founded if what was to happen was that medical evidence was to be given, but I and we are confining what counsel has to say to submissions, speaking as counsel, but, as I understand it, he can better express himself than perhaps Mr. D'Amato can because he is dealing with the medical aspect. We hear you as counsel, not as a medical practitioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, judge. May it please the court, my name is Dusan Vucicevic and I am co-counsel in this case and I will address the court as a counsel and not in any other capacity. Indeed, my background might help me to use the terminology in such a way that would help inform the court on what additional evidence will be forthcoming, if the court would that allow. As far as the new grounds for granting of provisional release based on being an exceptional circumstance, we have learned yesterday that perhaps a new condition has been discovered and we have not got an opportunity yet to talk to a medical doctor, and new condition, it could turn out to be a heart condition which we were informed by the detention facility authorities necessitates a further invasive investigation of the heart, which indeed it does carry some risk of mortality. Being that we are dealing with the accused who is a medical doctor himself, he understands the gravity of his situation. He, having been a model prisoner according to the warden, has for the first time thrown an irrational tantrum, being faced by an additional procedure. What basically he has done, he has to a degree given up a chance to be examined for evidence to be developed, and this is an extenuating circumstance which we would like to submit to the court. If I may propose --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I am sorry, just in clarification, you say he has given up an opportunity; you mean he refused to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: He refused to have any further testing, even knowing full well that a first symptom of this silent condition, but which has been discovered by a test, could be a sudden death, and the only way to diagnose this condition is for him to submit to a further testing and without prejudicing the decision of the court and not getting into medical, but just as background information, this procedure is called coronary angiography and such procedure the doctor is refusing to have. So what we would need is some time to have him talk to the family, to the doctors of his choice. We have the utmost confidence in the doctors of this country. They are, as we know in the States, some of the finest cardiologists in the world, but for any doctor to help a patient, we have to have a patient who is willing to receive that help. The conditions under which he is confined are indeed satisfactory to his Defence team. However, the lingering condition, psychological condition, under which he has been arrested have led to the change in his mind, and that is what, in combination, has led him to give up on his medical treatment. We all together have a problem, and the only problem is to either bring his family on an immediate basis here to counsel with him, his doctors that he prefers to counsel with him. We would not object to any of the procedure being done right now, and the doctor is perhaps -- as I have tried yesterday and we have made again tries to move him to the point that we all could find out what is going on, and then upon having angiography, then we can allow the expert in this field, the field of cardiology, to tell the court what his chances are and whether the chances -- indeed he has a bad heart, a large heart, the functional residual capacity of his heart is greatly diminished and he knows that, and when the chances of having operative surgery are indeed of that magnitude, whether it should be suggested strongly by his family and the doctors to have it or not to have it. That is the extenuating circumstance upon which the other elements which Mr. D'Amato is going to present shall rest upon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may quickly proceed then. We have a letter, and may I ask, sir, could you give these copies to the court? It is a letter from Republika Srpska that I would like to present instanter from the Prime Minister of Republika Srpska as follows, and let me read it for the record. This has to do with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You might wait until the copies have been distributed. There is a copy for the Prosecution, presumably?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Absolutely. There are two letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: You say there are two letters?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Yes, I handed him two letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: He made an error. One of the letters has one sentence on it, the other one has a full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: May I enter this language into the record or is that not necessary, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think we can accept these as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Would you mark them as such, Mr. Registrar? Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: The territorial government --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Perhaps before you go any further, you might just explain to us, the office held by the signatory of these two letters is?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Prime Minister of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It says "President".

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Would you explain the difference? It says "President".

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am Igor Pantelic, co-counsel. We have met before many times. Your Honour, I would like to clarify this letter. Simply it is a linguistic problem which we have to clarify. Prime Minister of Republika Srpska has his own Cabinet, his own space where he is acting, so there is not anything which is not in accordance with the rules and with the laws in Republika Srpska. It is just on the Serbian language formulation which specified about which we are speaking, so it is the government of Republika Srpska and he has his Cabinet. If you need further explanations, I am free to give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: We are saying that the word "President" is being translated here, but it is the equivalent in English of "Prime Minister", for the purposes of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What is the translation in English of "Prime Minister" then, or of "President", rather?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In Serbian language, "President" of government is equivalency as in English language "Prime Minister".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What is the English equivalent of "President" of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: President of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: These letters are only offered on a preliminary basis, because we are fully aware that under Rule 65 and other rules that this Tribunal would need to speak with a representative of the Republic, would have to work out conditions et cetera and all of that, documentation could be forthcoming, but we felt that to show the bona fides of the government's position, we would present this letter to you at the present time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before you can offer these letters, you have to make out this is one of the exceptional cases. You are basing your case for exceptional cases on medical grounds. You do not still have that certificate from the doctor to say he is refusing to get himself examined. It is really for him to show that exceptional circumstances exist in his favour. As long as that is sorted out, this discussion really would not be very relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: What Mr. Vucicevic was trying to say, I believe, was that under the conditions of the detention centre, given the way he was arrested and under the conditions there, he has no confidence, he is a man who is willing to die, he has lost psychological impetus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Would that make an exceptional circumstance?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: I think so, because the chance of him dying before this trial occurs are very high. I think if he were given medical treatment in his home town, by his own doctors, with his family, the support and all the psychological things that go with successful medical treatment, he could have this treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Unless he is examined, how do we know what sort of treatment is necessary for him?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: All of that would have to be given, your Honour. I am not trying to answer those kinds of questions now, I am only opening the door, if I may. Any submissions and any evidence that this court requires and wishes to consider, we will do our best to comply with that. This is not something that we have to deal with on the spur of the moment, we want to introduce and ask you for the kinds of evidence that you would need and the kinds of supporting documents that you need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that your client at the moment refuses to be examined medically? If that refusal continues, there will be no evidence upon which you can base your present application.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: What he refuses is an invasive procedure. In order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: What we would need would be, and I do not say that this would in any event be enough, but we would need medical evidence which establishes some real need for him to not be treated in the hospitals that are available here, but to return home, because really that is what your submission is, that he can only satisfactorily be treated for what is a life-threatening condition if he returns to his home and has the appropriate psychological support. That is in substance what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: In a sense, this is a test of a test. He has already received the tests that show that he has this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We have no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: All right. That is why we said it only happened yesterday. We will have to give you that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: So really what you would be seeking would be an adjournment of this application so that you can produce the appropriate evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Absolutely. I just wanted to sketch out the basis for that adjournment. Part of it I have given in the terms of these letters and the other part of it are the conditions that I would propose if the doctor were sent back to Prijedor. First of all, we would propose that he reports to NATO forces on a daily basis, in person. Secondly, we would propose that he would have a curfew, he could not leave his house during evening hours, you might say 10.00 pm to 6.00 am, or whatever you wish. Third, we would propose that he wear a monitoring device, so his physical movements could be monitored at all times. Fourth, we would propose that he be limited strictly to a geographic area, for example 50 kilometres radius of Prijedor or whatever the court wishes to impose, and finally we have a bond guaranteed by the government of Republika Srpska. So with the NATO forces present there, with this reporting, we think you will have every assurance in the world that the doctor will be available for trial and we would be glad to amplify on these provisions in the adjourned procedures that your Honour is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: How long would you be seeking by way of an adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Perhaps given the fact that this medical condition occurred only yesterday, these first tests, we would try to do it as expeditiously as possible, and leave it to your Honour's discretion perhaps to give us a reasonable time or perhaps to come back to you with a progress report or something of that nature. I think under the circumstances these things cannot be fitted into rigid legal categories but have to be dealt with more in a discretionary fashion. I do not have any proposal. Do you think there is a particular time period you would like to ask? We could perhaps begin -- suggestion of a two week adjournment, with a possibility of having to supplement that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no objection to an adjournment, because we are as anxious to find out about this medical condition as no doubt the Defence are. We raise no objection to that. I think I would reserve submissions on the other matters until such time as we hear the medical condition and the argument as it is fully ventilated, once we have that evidence. If the Defence need more than two weeks then we do not have any objection to that either, if it takes longer. I think the best thing to do is to find out what the medical condition is and we are anxious to ascertain whether he is going to be fit for trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: But it is not really satisfactory, is it, simply to adjourn for, say, two weeks and during that time to have the Defence and only the Defence get some medical examination of the accused. I would have thought that the Prosecution would also want to take part in that examination or to conduct an examination itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is quite right, your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Is there any need for arrangements to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In fact, we may seek an order that either we proceed by way of joint medical examination or alternatively, if the Defence wish to have their own medical examination separate from the Prosecution, that the accused submit himself to Prosecution examination, but I would hope, your Honour, that a joint medical examination could be a matter agreed upon, even if it means that the Defence have their doctor and we have ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: We appreciate the co-operation that we have received from the Prosecutor's Office all along and we believe this matter can be handled in a spirit of co-operation for the best results for the court and for the defendant and would be delighted to work out anything that you wish along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One thing, Mr. Niemann, that I think the bench would be assisted in, and that is the two letters that have been submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: They come from the government of the territory that you understand the accused would be returning to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Whether they come from a person authorised to commit the government or not is something I cannot comment upon at this stage, your Honour. It is certainly something that we will be pursuing, but on its face, it would appear to come from the government where the accused -- the government of the territory where the accused would be returning to, if he was to be given provisional release, your Honour. I might just perhaps -- one of the matters that occurred to me is that there has been a suggestion of reporting to NATO. The forces of NATO there, we would certainly have to consult them to see their attitude to this approach, so we would be arguing, your Honour, that their views on the matter would be relevant matters for consideration by the Tribunal, if your Honours were disposed to this course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Monitoring devices, they are available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We would need to investigate that as well, your Honour. I say all this, your Honour, but wish to emphasise that we are opposed to and will object to provisional release, but if your Honours were disposed to grant it, we would say that these matters are appropriate for consideration by the Chamber in any consideration of the matter which you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Will you be formally seeking an order of this Chamber at the time, if we do adjourn, for a joint medical examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: After discussion with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Perhaps I might have a discussion with Mr. D'Amato at some stage and get back before today's proceedings are concluded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I just wonder if it would be useful if we adjourn now for a quarter of an hour, for instance, to allow the two of you to discuss this and see what sort of procedure for a medical examination, assuming that the accused will submit himself to it, can be worked out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, your Honour. That would be very convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. D'Amato?

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I say one word? With respect to the NATO forces, with respect to the monitoring devices, we are only making suggestions. We are not insisting he has to report to NATO forces. We are just making the most precautionary suggestions, but those are up to the court to work out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: We will adjourn now. If in a quarter of an hour you have not been able to agree to a procedure, let us know and we will give you more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It might not be a bad idea to overcome any question of needing a Status Conference if at the same time you could discuss, Mr. Niemann, the question of amendment of the indictment so that we can wrap up the whole thing when we return.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: By all means, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Well gentlemen, what has been the outcome of the adjournment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have agreed that we will have an arrangement whereby either we jointly agree upon a psychiatrist and a cardiologist, and in the event of non-agreement that each party will appoint their own psychiatrist or cardiologist, as the case may be. We have discussed this with the Registrar and we, in conformity with the requirements of the Registrar, the Defence at their first given opportunity prepare, I understand, some questions which will be handed over to the Registrar so as to comply with their requirements. I do not know whether Mr. D'Amato --

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: That is fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the second question, we have not been able to be quite so successful in agreement. The position is, your Honours, that the Prosecution will seek to amend the indictment, and I can just outline briefly, there are two aspects to the indictment. There is an aspect which we would say is more formal in its nature, formality in its nature, it relates to lesser offences than the offence which has been charged, but there is a possibility of inclusion of a more substantive charge which would need to be supported by additional materials. We are in a position to proceed to deal with that relatively quickly, and we can do that. The difficulty that has been outlined by the Defence is that they wish an opportunity to present argument, I understand, to the confirming judge, if I understand their position correctly. We cannot see that as being available under the Rules. For our part, we are prepared not to seek to have the current indictment on which we are proceeding dismissed until such time as the Defence are given an opportunity to litigate the issue before the Trial Chamber, so in effect the position the Prosecution is prepared to proceed upon is that there will in effect be two indictments, the old indictment and what is in effect a new indictment, and that matter can come before the Trial Chamber and be litigated. That is the position the Prosecution is prepared to take in order to afford the Defence an opportunity to litigate this matter. We are not prepared to concede, and we do not concede it because of the Rules, the right of the Defence to appear before the confirming judge and to present argument at that juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Do I understand the Rules correctly then; until the trial begins, it is for the confirming judge to deal with any motion for amendment and that, in the terms of the Rules, seems to be an ex parte application by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. The basis upon which I say that we will not seek to dismiss the old indictment is that, of course, the Trial Chamber has the authority to say that it will not proceed on the new indictment, that it will only proceed on the old indictment, and that is the basis upon which we are prepared to afford them an opportunity to debate the issue should they wish to, after the confirmation of the new indictment. It is merely just a procedure so that they are not precluded from presenting argument should they wish to, but further than that we cannot go, because we say the rules do not contemplate a hearing before the confirming judge by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Yes. I think, Mr. D'Amato, that your attitude is that the Rules should do that, that was rather the gist of your motion to clarify. The fact is that the Rules at the moment do not afford you an opportunity on any amendment until the beginning of the actual trial. Amendments after that stage, of course, are matters upon which you would have an opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: I would like the court to rule, however, on the issue which has now come up for the first time, that the Prosecution seeks to amend this indictment by proceedings ex parte before Judge Odio Benito. If you want to make that ruling, I believe I would be then entitled to an interlocutory appeal on the question of whether that would be a sound ruling. Let me just for the record state two reasons why I believe that we ought to appear before Judge Odio Benito. After all, the arrest has now been -- has happened, the accused is in custody, and we are his attorneys, and it seems to me outrageously unfair for me to be prevented from appearing to defend my client's interest at any judicial stage in this matter, whether it is before Judge Odio Benito or anyone else. Ex parte hearings are utterly violative of my client's right to defend himself and therefore for that reason, no matter what the Rules say, this court cannot countenance a violation of my client's human rights to have his lawyers present at every relevant stage of the proceeding. Number two: in terms of judicial economy, why should Judge Odio Benito have to undergo great consideration on every aspect of the changes that the Prosecution may want in the indictment, only to have this court later rule on the validity of whether that proceeding should occur. It seems to me that in terms of judicial economy, Judge Odio Benito should be given a first chance to hear our arguments based on that ground and therefore -- and then set up a reviewable procedure, otherwise we have potential of a great deal of loss of time and energy, and that is a separate matter from the, I think, unconscionable ex parte aspect that is being here. I think this Tribunal has enough power, your Honour, to say that your interpretation of the Rules is that the trial has, so to speak, already begun once the accused is in detention. This is serious now. It is not as if he is at large and somebody is trying to amend an indictment before he has even heard about it. We are in the process of the trial here, even though these are technically called "preliminary matters". Therefore I think your interpretation of the Rules ought to afford us an opportunity to appear and contest any changes, especially the addition of new charges to this complaint, for all the substantive reasons that I would then go into at the appropriate time. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Well, we hear your submission, and I think in view of the views of my brother Judges it would be desirable to make no ruling here and now on what you say. That presents no real difficulty in view of the fact that we will be meeting again on the adjournment. As far as the date for the adjournment is concerned, Ms. Featherstone has pointed out that a fortnight's adjournment would be unsuitable, it would bring us to a day which is a dies non as far as this Tribunal is concerned, and it should be a three weeks' adjournment. If that is satisfactory to the parties, that will be Friday 31st . We will then deal with the matter you have raised. I do not know whether there is agreement as to the place of examination. Is there any problem about that? There is a hospital, I gather, in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There are facilities there, but I think this is a matter that surely can be resolved. If Mr. Kovacevic has to be taken to a hospital which has better facilities, I could not see that being a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: That can be done easily enough, can it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would add to that the fact that the Prosecution and the Defence are of one mind here, that the first thing to do is to serve the human needs of the client and to preserve his life and to preserve his health. That comes before any question of whether he is to be provisionally released or anything else. I think there is no difference of opinion whatsoever, we will in good spirit resolve all of these questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I can confirm that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: There is one procedural matter that perhaps we should draw to the attention of the Defence and that is that there was a grant of extension of time to file a motion challenging jurisdiction, and Ms. Featherstone, who keeps a close eye on these things, tells me that today is the last day for that. We felt that we should at least draw that to your attention so that it does not slip by.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I can say with all humility that I worked on that motion and it seemed to me, after doing the work, that it was unnecessary, that the Tadic judgement, that the rules I think would satisfy any doubts in my mind and therefore there would be no point in adding to the Tribunal's workload or wasting any time on the motion so with all respect, I retire that motion, but I appreciate your decision giving me the extension of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I think your decision was well taken. There is one matter that I would like to address both to you and also to Dr Kovacevic. Doctor, would you stand up? Doctor, you must understand that this motion now is based very substantially on your medical condition. To date, as I understand it, you have taken some objection to medical examination. If you wish this motion to proceed and to have some prospects of success, it is essential that you should be prepared to subject yourself to expert medical examination here. I just wanted to make that quite clear to you. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you. If there is nothing further at this stage, we may, I take it, adjourn until the 31st of this month.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The Chamber will now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: on Friday, 31st October 1997)
